title: Rabbi Yoshiyah of Usha
author: Aharon Hyman

paragraphs: It is very likely that he was Babylonian and studied there under Rav and Shmuel. Thus, in [Menachot 39a](https://www.sefaria.org/Menachot.39a), Rabba bar bar Chana says: “Rabbi Yoshiyah of Usha told me”—in Shmuel’s name. The Rabbi Yoshiyah who reports a teaching in Rav’s name in [Sukkah 2b](https://www.sefaria.org/Sukkah.2b.5) appears to be this Rabbi Yoshiyah of Usha.[^1]

He subsequently went up to the Land of Israel and became the leading authority at Usha. In [Gittin 33b](https://www.sefaria.org/Gittin.33b), Rabba bar bar Chana says: “We were five elders before Rabbi Yoshiyah of Usha.” In [Bekhorot 28b](https://www.sefaria.org/Bekhorot.28b), he says to Rabba bar bar Chana: “Come, and I will show you films on the eye that change.”[^2]

Were I not afraid to venture the suggestion, I would say that the text in [Berakhot 22a](https://www.sefaria.org/Berakhot.22a), “When Ravin came, he said: An incident occurred at Usha, in the entrance hall of Rav Oshaya,” should read “of Rabbi Yoshiyah.” The matter requires further examination.[^3]

notes.text: “Very likely” and “appears to be” preserve Hyman’s degrees of uncertainty. His proposed Babylonian origin, discipleship, and identification of the Sukkah speaker are his historical inferences, not independent determinations made by this translation. “Yoshiyah” corresponds to the Hebrew יאשיה, also commonly transliterated Josiah.

The accepted Hebrew witness cites **Sukkah 20b**, whereas the matching teaching in Rav’s name is **Sukkah 2b:5**, linked in the English. Its Bekhorot reference, **28b**, is correct. In the latter quotation the Hebrew witness has בהקין, while the linked Bavli reads בדוקין, films or opacities of the eye. The English follows the contextual sense; neither Hebrew witness is altered. “Leading authority” translates ריש; Hyman does not specify a formal office or succession in this sentence.

The replacement of Rav Oshaya with Rabbi Yoshiyah is **Hyman’s explicitly tentative emendation**. It is not the conventional wording of the linked Berakhot passage. His final וצ״ע, “the matter requires further examination,” is retained. The conventional Bavli reading and Hyman’s proposed reading therefore remain distinct.
